question: A research assistant aggregates outputs from five subagents (market sizing, competitor pricing, regulatory risk, customer sentiment, distribution channels) into one long combined document that is then passed to a synthesis step. The synthesis step's final memo omits the regulatory risk finding, which appeared in the third of five sections in the middle of the document. What is the best way to structure the aggregated input to prevent this in future runs?
options: A) Reorder the sections so the regulatory risk finding is always discussed last, since Claude retains the most recent content best
B) Instruct the synthesis step to read through the entire aggregated document twice before drafting its final memo
C) Place a short key-findings summary at the top of the aggregated document, then present each detailed section beneath an explicit heading
D) Split the aggregated document into two shorter documents, without adding any findings summary or section headers
correct_answers: C) Place a short key-findings summary at the top of the aggregated document, then present each detailed section beneath an explicit heading
explanations: Reordering to favor a single finding only protects that one item and still leaves every other middle section vulnerable in different runs.
Rereading does not reliably compensate for position effects and adds latency without a structural fix.

Correct — leading with a concise key-findings summary and using explicit section headers surfaces critical content regardless of where it originated, directly countering the middle-of-document drop-off.
Splitting the document without adding a summary or headers still leaves each half susceptible to internal middle-of-input drop-off.
